INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
The Alaska Legislative Council is a bipartisan,
constitutionally mandated permanent interim committee
and service agency of the Alaska State Legislature.
Comprised of the President of the Senate, the Speaker
of the House of Representatives, and twelve other
Senators and Representatives, the Council is vested
with broad authority to support and carry out
legislative functions, and between legislative sessions
it has the authority to engage in litigation on behalf of
the Alaska State Legislature.
The Alaska Legislative Council has a direct,
institutional interest in this case because the decision
below turns in significant part on the meaning and
purpose of statutes enacted by the Alaska State
Legislature, including the aircraft-forfeiture provision
codified at AS 04.16.220(a)(3)(C).  The Alaska Supreme
Court cited “the harm . . . addressed in the legislative
history of the forfeiture provision” when it evaluated
the gravity of the offense underlying the forfeiture.
Pet. App. 22a n.94.  The Alaska Supreme Court’s
excessive-fines analysis t hus rests on its understanding of what the Alaska State Legislature
intended when it enacted the local-option and
forfeiture statutes at issue.
Because Petitioner asks this Court to revisit that
analysis, this case requires the Court to consider
not only federal constitutional doctrine under the
Excessive Fines Clause, but also the historical context,

purpose, and scope of a specific Alaska statutory
scheme—the body of law the Legislative Council exists
to steward.  The Council submits this brief to assist the
Court in properly understanding the legislative record
as it bears on the quest ion presented, including
the history and context in which Alaska’s forfeiture
statute was enacted and the extensive findings on
which it is based.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
This Court has repeatedly recognized that “Alaska
is different.”  Sturgeon v. Frost, 587 U.S. 28, 32 (2019)
(quoting Sturgeon v. Frost, 577 U.S. 424, 438 (2016)).
This case vividly illustrates that principle.  Petitioner
Kenneth Jouppi, an air-taxi operator, was convicted
of knowingly transporting beer by airplane from
Fairbanks into Beaver, an Athabascan village with
roughly 80 residents that voted to prohibit the importation of alcoholic beverages.  Following Petitioner’s
conviction, Alaska law required the forfeiture of the
airplane he used to commit the offense.  Petitioner
asks this Court to hold t hat the forfeiture of his
airplane was an unconstitutionally excessive fine.
Resolving that question requires the Court to assess
the gravity of Petitioner’s offense, which in turn
requires understanding why the Alaska State Legislature mandated forfeiture of  aircraft used to smuggle
alcohol into dry villages in the first place.
The forfeiture provision at issue in this case was not
an isolated or reflexive response to a single incident.
It was the considered product of a stepwise, decadeslong process of seeking to understand and address the
harm that alcohol wrought on Alaska’s most remote
villages.  The detailed record before the Legislature
was not limited to population-wide statistics, although

3
there were more than enough  of those to identify a
genuine crisis.  The Legislature also heard individual
stories: testimony, letters, and firsthand accounts from
village residents, troopers, social workers, and public
safety officers describing the often-tragic consequences that alcohol visited upon individuals and
families.  These stories reinforced that where a village
lacks law enforcement to defuse a violent domestic
dispute or to rescue a child from abuse, and the only
road in or out is in the sky, even small quantities of
alcohol can have devastating consequences.
The legislative judgment underlying Alaska’s forfeiture provision was earned the hard way: village by
village, tragedy by tragedy.  The extensive record the
Legislature developed while investigating the problem
of alcohol in rural communities prompted it to act.  The
Legislature first enacted a law providing that villages
could choose to prohibit the sale and/or importation of
alcohol.  To reinforce that “local option,” the Legislature authorized, but did no t mandate, forfeiture of
aircraft and other vehicles used to smuggle alcohol
into communities that elected to go dry.  When that
proved ineffective, the Legislature stepped in again,
expanding villages’ authority to keep alcohol out by
permitting them to ban possession.  And when aircraft
operators persisted in transporting alcohol to villages
they knew were dry, the Legislature responded by
mandating the forfeiture of aircraft used to smuggle
alcohol into dry villages.
This Court has made clear that “judgments about
the appropriate punishment for an offense belong
in the first instance to the legislature.”  United States
v. Bajakajian , 524 U.S. 321, 336 (1998).  Indeed,
“constitutionally imposed uniformity” in punishments
is “inimical to traditional notions of federalism.”

4
Rummel v. Estelle, 445 U.S. 263, 282 (1980).  Here, the
Alaska State Legislature enacted a calibrated response
to a crisis unparalleled elsewhere.  It recognized that
the extraordinary isolation of rural Alaska villages,
coupled with the complete dearth of public-safety
infrastructure in many such communities, left residents uniquely vulnerable.  And it tailored the punishment to the conduct at issue: knowingly using an
aircraft to circumvent a community’s lawful choice
to prohibit alcohol.  That judgment readily satisfies
constitutional scrutiny.
ARGUMENT
I. Bajakajian confirms that courts owe
appropriate deference to legislative judgments concerning the gravity of criminal
offenses and the sanctions necessary to
address them.
This Court has made clear that the “touchstone of
the constitutional inquiry under the Excessive
Fines Clause is the principle of proportionality[.]”
Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 334; see id.  at 334–35
(recognizing that proportionality between the “amount
of the forfeiture” and the “gravity of the offense that it
is designed to punish” is “central[]” to the excessiveness inquiry).  Neither the te xt nor the history of the
Excessive Fines Clause addresses “how disproportional to the gravity of an offense a fine must be in
order to be deemed consti tutionally excessive.”  Id. at
336.  But this Court deemed two considerations
“particularly relevant” to that inquiry, including its
recognition that “judgments about the appropriate
punishment for an offense belong in the first instance
to the legislature.”  Id.  The Court has relied on this
principle in other cases interpreting the Eighth
Amendment.  See Solem v. Helm , 463 U.S. 277,

5
290 (1983) (explaining that courts “should grant
substantial deference to the broad authority that
legislatures necessarily po ssess in determining the
types and limits of punishments for crimes”).
This Court has also recognized that federalism plays
a role in determining whether a punishment is
“grossly disproportionate” to an offense.  In Rummel v.
Estelle, 445 U.S. 263, the Court explained that even if
a penal statute were “the most stringent found in the
50 States,” its severity “hardly would render [the
defendant’s] punishment ‘grossly disproportionate’ to
his offenses or to the punishment he would have
received in the other States.”  Id. at 281; see id. at 281–
82 (collecting examples of severe punishments for
crimes thought to be “particularly reprehensible” in
various states).  To the contrary, “[a]bsent a constitutionally imposed uniformity inimical to traditional
notions of federalism, some State[s] will always bear
the distinction of treating particular offenders more
severely than any other State.”  Id. at 282.
As the discussion below reveals, the Alaska State
Legislature compiled an extensive record documenting
the harms caused by alcohol in remote villages and the
ways aircraft operators undermined local alcohol bans
by continuing to transport alcohol into those communities.  The solution it devised—mandatory forfeiture of
aircraft used to transport alcohol into dry villages—
should be afforded the “substantial deference” it is due.
Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 336 (quoting Solem, 463 U.S.
at 290).

6
II. The Alaska State Legislature acted in
response to a documented public safety
crisis of extraordinary severity.
A. The Legislature enacted its local-option
and forfeiture statutes in 1980 in
response to studies documenting the
toll of alcoholism and alcohol-related
crime, particularly in rural communities.
Alaska villages have suffered, and fought back
against, the harms wrought by alcohol since Alaska’s
territorial days.2  In the 1960s, village leaders were
informed that they did not have the authority to ban
alcohol under state law.  Laurie H. Otto, A Search for
Control: The Effect of Alcohol on Public Rights and
Private Wrongs —Report to the Legislature Joint
Special Committee on Local Option Laws 20 (1986).
Attempting to enact or enfo rce such a ban—even if a
rural village believed that doing so was in its own best

in Fairbanks and ended up in the villages.  See id. at 107 (noting
that at Chena Village “[t]he natives buy their whiskey in

7
interest—could subject village leaders to arrest.  Id. at
20–21.  At the same time, villages were denied access
to preventative law enforcement that might have
reduced the worst of the consequences related to
alcohol overconsumption.  Stephen Conn, No Need of
Gold—Alcohol Control Laws and the Alaska Native
Population: From the Russians Through the Early
Years of Statehood, Univ. of Alaska Anchorage, Sch. of
Just. 60 (1986); see also Governor’s Comm’n on the
Admin. of Just., Standards and Goals for Criminal
Justice 13 (1976) (observing that state law had
“eliminated the authority and responsibility of
traditional Native units of government such as village
councils to act in criminal justice matters,” leaving
“most communities of ru ral Alaska without the
protection of any form of criminal justice service”).
In 1972, Alaska adopted the Uniform Alcoholism
and Intoxication Treatment Act, which decriminalized
public drunkenness in favor of treatment.  See Peter
v. State , 531 P.2d 1263, 1271 (Alaska 1975). That
approach was workable in cities with detoxification
and other treatment facilities.  See Governor’s Comm’n
on the Admin. of Just., supra, at 2.  But in rural Alaska
villages, an incapacitated person without services and
nowhere to go “would quickly freeze to death.”  Otto,
supra, at 23 (quoting Kim L. Moeller, Alcohol Abuse
and the Police in Rural Alaska: the North Slope
Borough and City of Barrow Experience (2d ed. Jan.
1979)).  Recognizing the unique realities of life in
remote villages, a 1976 report recommended that
“village life must be governed by village law and
custom as much as possible,” including with respect to
the regulation of alcohol.  Governor’s Comm’n on the
Admin. of Just., supra, at 14.

8
The Alaska State Legislature took up that charge.
The Legislature recognized that most remote villages
had no organized municipal government and thus had
no practical way to restrict or prohibit alcohol within
their own communities.  The Legislature also understood that the needs and preferences of individual
communities varied, and that imposing a blanket
prohibition from Juneau would have failed to account
for those differences.  See id. (setting a goal that “in
rural Alaska there will be  local decision making
authority in each village in such basic areas as . . .
alcohol control”).  So in 1980, the Legislature considered a bill (SB 239) that ga ve “established village[s]”
the option to regulate alcohol—what became known as
a “local option.”  S.B. 239, 11th Leg., 1st Reg. Sess.
(Alaska 1979); SLA 1980, ch. 131, § 3. 3  The bill’s
sponsor told the Senate Judiciary Committee that the
provision was meant to provide villages with greater
autonomy to “dry[] out,” if that is what the village
elected to do.  Minutes, S. Judiciary Comm., at 1–2
(Jan. 31, 1980), https://www.akleg.gov/library/Subjec

both the House and Senate.  1980 Alaska House
Journal 2121–22; 1980 Alaska Senate Journal 1658.

graduated options to limit alcohol.  AS 04.11.502(a)–

licensed community establishments, AS 04.11.492
(1980), or holders of selected license types, AS
04.11.500 (1980); or prohibi t both the sale and
importation of alcoholic beverages, AS 04.11.496
(1980).  The choice was entrusted to local voters via
referendum elections.  See Harrison v. State, 687 P.2d
332, 336 (Alaska Ct. App. 1984).

the Administration of Justice had identified alcohol as
the State’s first-priority criminal justice problem.  See
Governor’s Comm’n on the Admin. of Just., supra, at 1

III. After alcohol continued to devastate rural
Alaska, the Legislature expanded local
control and investigated the role of
aircraft in transporting alcohol to remote

The 1980 local-option law represented a significant
transfer of authority from th e state to local villages.
But by the mid-1980s, it was becoming clear that the
reforms had not fully achieved their purposes.  Alcohol
was still finding its way into dry communities.  And
once alcohol reached these communities, it continued
to wreak the same tragic consequences that had
catalyzed the 1980 code revisions in the first place.
A. In 1986, the Legislature authorized
villages to ban alcohol possession.
Three years after the enactment of the 1980 localoption and vehicle-forfeiture laws, the Legislature
authorized a study of the local-option law.  The
resulting report described alcohol as “the most
significant public health problem in rural Alaska.”

and explained that they had “told the airlines that fly into Beaver
not to haul anyone who is carrying booze or is under the
influence.”  Id.

25
into a local-option village), whatever the quantity of
alcohol and whatever the defendant’s criminal record.
AS 04.16.220(i)(1).  By contrast, forfeiture of a
watercraft or other motor vehicle is mandatory only
where the defendant has a prior violent felony
conviction, is on felony probation or parole, has a prior
bootlegging conviction, or transported at least twice
the amount of alcohol meeting the statutory threshold
for an intent-to-sell offense.   AS 04.16.220(i)(2).  As the
context in which the provision was enacted makes
plain, the Legislature “viewed the gravity of aircraftfacilitated importation as  more severe than other
methods of unlawful importation.”  Pet. App. 20a.
Second, the law provides that where a watercraft or
other motor vehicle would otherwise be subject to
mandatory forfeiture, a court need not order forfeiture
if the vehicle or watercraft is “the sole means of transportation for a family residing in a village,” provided
the court made certain findings.  AS 04.16.220(j)(1).
Testimony during legislative hearings indicated
that the exception covers “a car, truck, snowmachine,
fourwheeler, or watercraft.”  CS for Senate Bill 170
(JUD), Sectional Summary , at 10 (Apr. 5, 2004),
available in  Senate Finance Committee Bill File for
SB 170, https://www.akleg.gov/library/AS%20compilat
ions/AS%2012/AS%2012.55.%20127%20and%20145/A
S%2012.55.127(c)(2)(F)/SB%20170%20(2004)/SFIN23
%20SB%20170.pdf.  The exception demonstrates that
the Legislature considered and accounted for the
hardship forfeiture can cause a village family who
might rely on a boat or snowmachine to hunt, fish, haul
water and fuel, or travel to the next village downriver.
But the Legislature omitted aircraft from the exception.
The Legislature also ensured that innocent parties
would not face forfeiture.  The statute makes man-

26
datory forfeiture expressly “subject to remission to
innocent parties.”  AS 04.16.220(i).  An owner, or a
person holding a lien, mortgage, or conditional sales
contract, may recover the property by showing that he
(1) was not a party to the v iolation, (2) had “no actual
knowledge or reasonable cause to believe” that the
property would be used unl awfully, and (3) had no
actual knowledge or reasonable cause to believe
that the user had a criminal record for Title 4
violations or had committed other Title 4 violations.
AS 04.16.220(e)–(f).  This safe harbor ensures that
only those who “turn a blind eye” will lose their
property.  Minutes, S. Judiciary Comm., SB 170, at 8
(Mar. 10, 2004).
V. The Alaska State Legislature’s calibrated
response fit the state’s unique needs and
challenges, and directly addressed the
problem the Legislature was trying to solve.
As the legislative history described above indicates,
the Alaska State Legislature was well informed of the
problem it sought to solve.   It faced a public-safety
crisis that presented challenges rarely, if ever,
encountered elsewhere in the Nation.  It knew the
hardships attendant to village life, including the lack
of law enforcement available to assist in a crisis.  It
recognized the importance of self-determination for
the villages, mostly populated by Alaska Native
people, that sought to stem the tide of alcohol—and the
associated waves of illness and violence—entering
their communities.  And it learned of the pilots like
Petitioner who ignored local  bans and continued to
deliver alcohol to villages that eschewed it.
The Legislature’s approach was incremental and
measured: modest at first, growing more robust as the
problem continued unabated.  Its policy judgment that

27
aircraft forfeiture was an appropriate punishment was
based on the evidence before it—including evidence
that the risk of forfeiture would deter carriers from
transporting alcohol into dry villages.  That judgment
is entitled to this Court’s deference.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the Court should affirm.
